name: Pachyonychia Congenita

criteria.description: Presence of hypertrophic nail dystrophy affecting fingernails and toenails
Painful focal plantar keratoderma with callus formation
Oral leukokeratosis presenting as white plaques on oral mucosa
Follicular hyperkeratosis with keratotic papules on extensor surfaces
Identification of pathogenic variants in keratin genes KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT16, or KRT17

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of hypertrophic nail dystrophy and plantar keratoderma plus genetic confirmation or clinical features consistent with PC in absence of genetic testing
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing is recommended for confirmation but diagnosis can be clinical based on characteristic features.

pathognomonic.notes: Thickened, discolored, and distorted nails typically present from infancy
Callus formation on pressure points of the soles causing significant pain
White plaques on oral mucosa, often asymptomatic

common.notes: Keratotic papules on extensor surfaces such as elbows and knees
Excessive sweating of palms and soles
Blisters may develop especially in infancy or early childhood
searchTerms: blister formation on hands and feet

common.notes: Epidermal inclusion cysts or steatocystomas commonly develop

occasional.notes: Periodic shedding of nails may occur
Sparse or brittle hair reported in some cases
Rare involvement of laryngeal mucosa causing voice changes
Thickening of palmar skin may be present

rare.notes: Multiple sebaceous cysts, especially in PC-K17 subtype

rare.symptomName: Nail fungal infections secondary to dystrophy
rare.notes: Secondary infections due to nail abnormalities
searchTerms: nail fungus due to nail damage

laboratory: Histopathology showing epidermal hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis
imaging: Not typically required; imaging may be used to evaluate cysts if present
genetic: Pathogenic variants in KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT16, or KRT17 genes
other: Clinical examination revealing characteristic nail and skin changes

distinguishingFeatures: Fungal infection confirmed by microscopy or culture
Lack of plantar keratoderma and oral leukokeratosis
Usually affects nails without systemic features
Blistering primarily due to mechanical trauma
Genetic mutations in keratin 5 or 14 genes
Different genetic causes and inheritance patterns

redFlags: Severe painful plantar keratoderma impairing ambulation
Rapid progression of nail dystrophy with secondary infection
Airway obstruction symptoms due to laryngeal involvement
references: Smith FJD, et al. Pachyonychia congenita: clinical features, molecular genetics, and diagnosis. J Invest Dermatol. 2019.
